top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Grossman, with the citation confined to the political economy of trade protection) is the strongest option. It is a single, coherent discovery: lobbying and tariff formation became a tractable equilibrium object that generated about thirty years of theory, testing and trade-agreement analysis. Attribution is the cleanest on the slate, since a tightly coupled two-person programme excludes no co-originator at the same level, and maturity is not in doubt. The main reservation is the mixed, specification-sensitive empirical record of protection-for-sale. I treat the contribution as an organising framework and research programme, not a confirmed quantitative result, so the citation should not imply validation or reach into the growth strand. I rank P002 second. With the stable Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio and a citation limited to trade-shock evidence on labour demand, it is defensible, but persistence and shift-share identification are still being re-estimated and the task-framework antecedents are uncredited. I rank P003 third. Its empirical confrontation is dense, but the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum attribution gap cannot be closed within three names and the case rests heavily on one 2003 paper. All three are substantive contributions, so I rank each above no award (P000). My ordering rests on common criteria of achievement, maturity, attribution and citation scope, not on how many colleagues support each proposal.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Helpman, Grossman, Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Melitz. Per profile, Hassler (chair) and Boppart are long-time co-authors and IIES colleagues, and both support P001. That is a tie between committee members, not a candidate-specific conflict. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
